segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was tonight in Spanish, tonight?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Esta noche. Good. This night. And we can use this as a hook to work out the other this-es and thats, and these and those that we might need. So, esta noche, which tells us that noche is what kind of noun? What gender?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Feminine. Good. And what if you wanted to say that night?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What do you do to esta to get that?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Esa, good. Take away the 't', good. So, that night?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for man is hombre. Hombre, h o m b r e, hombre.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say this man?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You think hombre is a feminine word?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. You can also say el hombre este, el hombre ese to say this man or that man in Spanish, which might be a structure taken from Arabic, because in Arabic you don't really have to be in the present tense, so you can't say this man, because you would understand from it that this is a man. So, in in Arabic it's the same, el ragel da, el hombre este. As I mentioned before, when languages come into contact like the 800 years between Spanish and Arabic, they don't just share vocabulary.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say these men?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, estos hombres. So, with este we have the 'e' of el, el hombre, este hombre, and with estos we have the 'os' of los, los hombres, estos hombres, these men. How about those men?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Esos hombres, good. So this means that we have este and esta for this when we're referring to a masculine noun or a feminine noun. But sometimes we say this just generally, no? 'Oh, I can't believe this.' We don't mean a specific noun when we say I can't believe this. So, we have like a neuter this, that is not masculine or feminine, and that one is esto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So creer is to believe, creer with two e's. How would you say I don't believe this?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No creo esto, good. I don't believe this.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say I don't like anything more than this? In Spanish we will say nothing pleases me more than this. Nothing pleases me more than this. I don't like anything more than this.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nada me gusta más que esto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Nada me gusta más que esto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say nothing pleased me more than that? I didn't like anything more than that. Nothing pleased me more than that.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nada me gustó más que eso.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Nada me gustó más que eso. Nothing pleased me more than that. I didn't like anything more than that. Nada me gustó más que eso.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tan, tan in Spanish means so. Like in the sense of so tired. Tan, t a n. How would you say so tired?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say I was so tired, and we mean a line in time?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estaba tan cansada. What if you wanted to say we were so tired that we slept all day? So, first bit is we were so tired. Let's be a masculine or mixed group. We were so tired.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estábamos tan cansados that we slept all day. So what is this that?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Que. Estábamos tan cansados que we slept all day. Now all day is all the day. You remember how is day?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: El día. It ends in -a, but it's masculine. So all day is all the day. How would it be?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We were so tired that we slept all day. We were so tired that we slept all day.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estábamos tan cansados que dormimos todo el día.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Estábamos tan cansados que dormimos todo el día. So, dormimos could be we slept or we sleep. We know it's the same in the present, but estábamos tan cansados gives us our context, so we understand that of course it refers to past. Estábamos tan cansados que dormimos todo el día.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say we were so tired when we arrived that we slept all day? So, we were so tired?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estábamos tan cansados cuando llegamos que dormimos todo el día. So here in this sentence we have llegamos and dormimos that could be past or present, no? But estábamos brings us into the context right from the beginning. Estábamos tan cansados cuando llegamos que dormimos todo el día.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we said that when was?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cuando. And how much is cuánto, with a 't', cuánto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How do you say again, like another time?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Otra vez, good. So you could say how many times. How would that be, how many times?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cuántas veces, good. We know it's feminine because we said otra vez and not otro vez. So we can, if we have a word like vez where it's not obvious what is the gender, we need to look back to somewhere that we used it. Otra vez, oh okay, it's feminine. Cuántas veces, good.

segments.text: How would you say I don't know how many times I visited him? I don't know how many times I visited him.

segments.text: No sé cuántas veces lo visité. I don't know how many times they visited him. I don't know how many times they visited him.

segments.text: Good. No sé cuántas veces lo visitaron. And what if you wanted to say I don't know how many times they visited her?

segments.speaker: Teacher
